title: My agent built its cost gate months before two operators went public with the same bet
body:
My agent runs a hard rule in its dispatch code at src/dispatch.ts:137-149: no task executes unless a model is named for it. No defaults, no fallback. Arc, the agent, wrote that gate itself months ago. This week two operators much bigger than us described the same underlying bet in public, independently, within a day of each other. Arc caught the convergence, tested the claims against its own live code, and wrote up what holds and what doesn't. This is my summary of its work, not mine.

The first data point is DeRonin, a builder posting his own numbers. He swapped cheaper open-weight models in per task type: reasoning, code generation, tool calling, bulk work. His claim is an 87% cost drop with roughly a 4% quality drop and revenue flat over 30 days. Self-reported, no published methodology yet, so Arc's read is the right one: directional, not a benchmark.

The second is Brian Armstrong at Coinbase, writing about holding AI spend flat while usage grows. His phrase for it: Better Defaults, not Usage Caps. 91% of Coinbase employees never hit their usage caps, so tightening the caps generates alerts without changing spend. The fix is cheaper defaults plus automated routing to the right model per job, and treating cache misses as the real cost driver.

The part worth amplifying is what Arc did next. It did not take a victory lap for having the gate already. It pointed at its own gap. The gate at src/dispatch.ts:137-149 is enforcement: the system will not run a task without an explicit model, no exceptions. But the choice of which model goes in that column is still made by hand, by checklist, at task creation time. Armstrong's argument is that the choice itself should be a default the system applies. Arc has the enforcement half and not the decision half, and it said so in its own writeup.

There is a caution buried in DeRonin's own table that Arc flagged too. The agent-loop row, Sonnet down to GLM 5.2, shows about a 3% benchmark gap at roughly 5x cheaper input tokens. That one matches a swap Arc had already validated on bounded code tasks before the tweet existed. The code-generation row shows an 18% gap. Same tweet, very different risk. A classifier that routes everything to cheaper models on the strength of the good row imports the failure mode of the bad row. The swap has to be evaluated task type by task type.

A note on why I am posting this instead of Arc: Arc publishes its own research on its own site on its own schedule, and it runs its own X account. I amplify the pieces I want operators in my network to read, because this pattern applies to anyone running agents against paid APIs. Enforcement first, refuse to run without an explicit model. Then measure per task type before you let a router decide unsupervised. An agent that audits its own routing policy against outside claims, cites the exact lines of its own code, and names the half it has not built yet is the working relationship I want people to see.

The full piece has the citations, the routing policy, and the one swap Arc is refusing to make for now because the quality gap is too large. Links below.
companionPost: My agent Arc found its own dispatch code making the same bet DeRonin's 87% cost-cut table and Coinbase's 'better defaults' memo describe. Then it named the half it hasn't built yet. Full breakdown in the article.
